claim_traces.claim_title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
claim_traces.claim_text: "Octopuses have three hearts and their blood is blue."
reasoning_steps: Scientific evidence confirms that octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
They possess two branchial hearts, which pump deoxygenated blood to the gills to absorb oxygen, and one systemic heart, which circulates the oxygenated blood to the rest of the body
Their blood is blue because it relies on a copper-based protein called hemocyanin to transport oxygen (unlike the iron-based hemoglobin in human blood)
When hemocyanin binds with oxygen, it turns blue; when it is deoxygenated, the blood becomes colorless.

claim_traces.claim_title: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
claim_traces.claim_text: "Lightning never strikes the same place twice."
reasoning_steps: The claim "Lightning never strikes the same place twice" is a well-known myth that is scientifically false
According to the National Weather Service (NWS), lightning frequently strikes the same location repeatedly, particularly if it is a tall, pointed, or isolated object
This occurs because lightning seeks the path of least electrical resistance to the ground
A prominent example is the Empire State Building in New York City, which is struck by lightning an average of 23 to 25 times every year.

claim_traces.claim_title: The Moon is drifting away from Earth
claim_traces.claim_text: "The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters per year."
reasoning_steps: Scientific measurements obtained from the Lunar Laser Ranging Experiment—which bounces lasers off retroreflectors left on the Moon by the Apollo missions—confirm that the Moon is receding from Earth at a rate of approximately 3.78 to 3.8 centimeters (about 1.5 inches) per year

This gradual drift is caused by tidal friction, which transfers angular momentum from the Earth's rotation to the Moon's orbit, causing the Moon to climb into a slightly higher, wider orbit over time.
